blocks.text: Throughout October 2026, we identified an actor using tooling associated with ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration-testing agent, to target multiple IT and software vendors. The activity focused on identity providers (Okta, Entra, Cognito) and abuse of Microsoft 365 integrations. We observed repeated attempts to uncover authentication bypasses, enumerate APIs, and access customer data (of the targeted vendors) across multiple environments.

blocks.text: ARTEX is an open-source autonomous penetration testing framework. A Chinese developer published it on GitHub in July 2026, and it won Baidu's "Agent+" red team challenge that September. In practice, an operator supplies a target and an objective. A planner agent then chooses the next step, worker agents run tools like nmap, curl, and Impacket, and every result feeds a shared graph of assets and findings.

blocks.text: Across the investigated environments, we observed a consistent sequence of reconnaissance and attack attempts:

inlines.text: Across the investigated environments, we observed a consistent sequence of reconnaissance and attack attempts:
Download JavaScript bundles, exposed source maps, runtime configurations, and Swagger/OpenAPI documentation to discover internal API routes and application functionality.
Repeatedly initiate sign-in flows, manipulate OAuth callbacks and state parameters, test unsigned JWTs, and probe SSO and Microsoft 365-specific endpoints.
Attack identity providers and login flows:
Password-spray corporate Okta and Entra ID environments, and target internal and proprietary application login pages.
Repeatedly invoke password-reset, username-recovery, activation, and reset-token endpoints.
Register accounts using disposable email addresses where possible, then manipulate predictable identifiers to probe for broken access controls and unauthorized cross-tenant data access.
Rotate IP addresses when blocked, and constantly circulate user agents.

A unique user-agent string was assigned to each burst, distinct from those used in previous waves.
The median gap between authentication attempts was strictly one second.
Individual bursts lasted anywhere from 20 to 60 minutes.
The agent primarily focused on accounts belonging to software engineers.
Some individual users were subjected to more than a dozen login attempts.

blocks.text: The activity was persistent and highly automated. Some sessions lasted 24–30 hours, and when IPs were blocked, new addresses appeared within minutes.

blocks.text: In one session, the agent cycled through a dozen variations of the same SSO endpoint (/sso, /sso/, /sso/login, /sso/jwt, /jwt/sso…), each with and without the same forged token, at a rate of about one request per second. When a login page started rate-limiting the activity, the agent simply switched to a different endpoint on the same host and carried on.

blocks.text: Although most of these attempts failed, the true threat lies in the methodology. While a human attacker is bound by time constraints and fatigue, an autonomous agent does not give up. It simply continues to iterate until it finds a single weak point.

blocks.text: None of the individual techniques observed are novel. However, together the agent behind this attack is illuminated. There are a few clear signals:

inlines.text: None of the individual techniques observed are novel. However, together the agent behind this attack is illuminated. There are a few clear signals:
: when sign-up was open, it registered with a disposable mailbox, confirmed the account, and immediately requested another company's data.
Each automated step used the output of the last one
: internal API routes are called by name minutes after pulling the source maps
: when a login page started rate-limiting, the agent moved to a different endpoint on the same host. When an IP was blocked, a new one appeared within minutes.
: a human attacker of this skill level is unlikely to spend their time testing generic payloads on the heavily scrutinized Microsoft OAuth flows.
